title: Wearable Organic Electrochemical Transistor Biosensor for Real-Time Measurement of Sweat Salinity and Saturation
authors: Francesco Gentile; Edmondo Battista; Daniela Cardone; David Perpetuini; Teresa Paolucci; Mirko Pesce; Ayub Alam; Valentina Vit; Luigi Bruno; Arcangelo Merla; Nicola Coppedé
matched_keywords: organic electrochemical transistor; oect; conductive polymer; pedot:pss; electrochemical transistor; biosensor
abstract: Abstract Wearable sweat sensing offers a noninvasive strategy for continuous monitoring of hydration, electrolyte balance, and physiological stress. Here, we demonstrate a flexible textile-based organic electrochemical transistor (OECT) biosensor for real-time quantification of sweat salinity and saturation during physical activity. The device consists of cotton fibers functionalized with the conductive polymer PEDOT:PSS, configured as channel and gate electrodes within a biocompatible patch. The gate and drain currents measured by the device in response to sweat are decoded using a mathematical model that estimates both the total salt concentration and the sweat saturation level. Unlike conventional enzymatic or membrane-based sensors, the platform operates without selective coatings, improving robustness, reproducibility, and mechanical stability. In in vitro tests, the device exhibited a linear response in the 10–4 M–1 M concentration range, a limit of detection as low as 10-5 M, and a response time below 40 s. Moreover, the sensor device was validated in three participants during treadmill running sessions lasting up to 1 h. The saturation profiles derived from the sensor showed a very high correlation with facial skin temperature measured by infrared thermography in all participants (up to 0.90), and with heart rate variability (HRV) derived from ECG recordings in two of the three participants (up to 0.86). Cross-correlation analysis revealed that the time lag between the onset of the exercise-induced increase in body temperature and the onset of sweating ranges from 600 to 740 s, in line with values predicted by the literature. These results demonstrate accurate, sensitive, and continuous tracking of sweat dynamics in real time. The proposed wearable OECT platform establishes a robust foundation for biomedical applications including monitoring of hydration disorders, electrolyte imbalance, metabolic dysfunction, and autonomic dysregulation.

title: Inhibition of Oxidative Activity by Photo-induced Surface Hydroxyl Groups in Bismuth Titanium Oxide Photocatalysts Detected by Single-Molecule Fluorescence Imaging
authors: William H. Rackers; Han Zhang; Zachary B. Ben-Meir; Bryce Sadtler
abstract: Abstract The surface structure of semiconductor photocatalysts plays a critical role in the extraction of charge carriers during photocatalytic reactions. However, the surface structures of many photocatalysts are dynamic under catalytic conditions, which makes identifying photo-induced changes and their effect on photocatalytic activity challenging. Herein, we use super-resolution, single-molecule fluorescence imaging to map the spatial distribution of catalytically active regions and quantify the changes in activity of those regions for photocatalytic oxidation in bismuth titanium oxide (Bi4Ti3O12) nanoplates. Individual nanoplates varied widely in both activity and stability, reflecting significant heterogeneity among a single synthesis batch of photocatalyst particles. We observed that while the nanoplates are more active around the perimeter of the basal facet, those perimeter regions decrease in activity at the same relative rate as the rest of the basal facet, indicating a spatially uniform degradation mechanism. Through ensemble structural characterization of the nanoplates after irradiation, we identified surface hydroxyl groups as the photo-induced feature. Our results indicate that surface hydroxyl groups introduce hole trap states that increase charge recombination at the surface of the nanoplates, leading to the observed decrease in activity. Surprisingly, we identified nanoscale features that do not begin with high activity but exhibit a slower rate of activity loss, leading to regions with greater activity relative to the rest of the basal facet at the end of imaging. Our findings highlight the importance of not only understanding how different nanoscale features influence catalytic activity but also how these features evolve over time, which dictates catalyst stability.
